newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani leaders meet before verdict on Bhutto.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani leaders meet before verdict on Bhutto.

text.p: Pakistan's powerful Council for Defence and National Security, grouping government and military leaders, met on Tuesday before a decision by the Supreme Court on whether to reinstate ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto.

The official APP news agency said the court would rule on Wednesday on whether to restore Bhutto's government and the National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, or uphold their November 5 dismissal by President Farooq Leghari.
If the court rejects Bhutto's plea and backs Leghari's action, elections set for February 3 will go ahead.

The 10-man council, which is headed by Leghari and includes caretaker Prime Minister Meraj Khalid and chiefs of the armed forces, "reviewed in depth the measures taken to ensure that the elections were held...in a free, fair and impartial manner", a government statement said.

It did not say whether the controversial council, set up to advise the government on important matters, discussed Bhutto's plea. But newspaper reports said before the meeting that it would consider the implications of Bhutto's restoration as prime minister.

Leghari set up the council earlier this month, giving the armed forces' chiefs a formal advisory role in government affairs. Most Pakistani political leaders opposed the creation of the council, saying it would undermine parliament and the cabinet.
Bhutto wants the Supreme Court to overturn her dismissal by Leghari, who accused her government of corruption, nepotism, extra-judicial killings and contempt for the judiciary.

Leghari has said the elections would be halted if the court restored the assembly. He told the Cable News Network television on Monday that he might step down if the court overturned Bhutto's dismissal.
Tuesday's meeting of the council, the second since its formation on January 6, also reviewed steps taken by the government to prevent violence on polling day and to stimulate the economy.
It said the council "noted that the economic condition had stabilised but that sustained effort over a period of time was required before the structural reforms bore fruit".
The government says the council can give only non-binding advice on issues such as defence, national security and financial policies, and its creation has not violated the constitution.

Bhutto and other critics of Leghari have accused the president of once again dragging the armed forces into politics after military rule for nearly half of Pakistan's existence since its creation during the partition of India in 1947.
